item.title: Pentagon says all fighter jets are safe after Iran claims it hit an F-16
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Talks between the U.S. and Iran remain stalled despite the two countries signing a memorandum of understanding in June, aimed at ending the war that began with joint American-Israeli strikes on the country in February. The opening strikes killed a host of top Iranian officials and commanders, among them Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. The two sides have continued to exchange strikes, though have not returned to the intense fighting seen in the early stages of the conflict. The U.S. says it is enforcing a naval blockade of the country's Persian Gulf and Gulf of Oman ports, while Iran claims control over the strategic Strait of Hormuz and continues to claim attacks on shipping transiting the waterway. Meanwhile, intensified fighting between Saudi-backed Yemeni forces and Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen has seen the latter repeatedly attack Saudi military, oil infrastructure and transport facilities. See the most recent developments below. Latest Developments Nov 22, 7:34 AM Regional nations condemn Iranian attack on Bahrain Saudi Arabia, Kuwait and Qatar issued statements on Sunday condemning Iran's attack on Bahrain on Saturday, which Manama said injured two people and caused a file at a civilian industrial facility. Qatar's Foreign Ministry said the attack constituted a "flagrant violation of its sovereignty and territorial integrity, and a blatant breach of international law, the United Nations Charter, and the principles of good neighborliness." The Saudi Foreign Ministry described the attack as "heinous" and said it holds Iran responsible for the consequences of its continued perpetration of these flagrant attacks." Kuwait's Foreign Ministry said that Iranian attacks on Bahrain "threaten the region's security and stability." Social Media via Reuters - PHOTO: Flames rise as fire breaks out at a civilian facility, following what Bahrain says was an Iranian attack, in Sitra, Bahrain, on Nov. 21, 2026, in this still image obtained from a social media video. Nov 22, 5:42 AM IRGC claims shooting down of US drone Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps on Sunday claimed to have shot down a U.S. MQ-1 Predator drone east of the Strait of Hormuz. The IRGC made its claim in a statement carried by the state-run IRNA News Agency. U.S. Central Command did not immediately comment on the IRGC claim. Nov 22, 4:56 AM Saudi Arabia intercepts Houthi drone targeting Riyadh, spokesperson says Saudi forces intercepted a drone launched by the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen toward the Saudi capital Riyadh on Sunday, military spokesperson Col. Turki Al-Maliki said in a post to X. Nov 22, 4:51 AM 2 people injured in Iranian attack on Bahrain, ministry says Bahrain's Interior Ministry said in a post to X on Sunday that two people were injured in an Iranian attack on the kingdom on Saturday. One Bahraini citizen was injured and is in a stable condition, while one Pakistani citizen was injured as is in a critical condition, the ministry said. Both injured people are being treated in hospital, it added. Nov 22, 4:24 AM Iran says Bahrain attacks targeted US Patriot sites The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps claimed late on Saturday that its latest attacks on Bahrain targeted two American Patriot surface-to-air missile systems at the al-Riffa air base and the Sakhir air base, according to a statement carried by the state-run IRNA News Agency. Nov 21, 3:26 PM Bahrain says Iranian attack caused fire at industrial facility Bahrain said an Iranian attack caused at a fire at a civilian industrial facility on Saturday. "Civil Defence is working to bring the fire under control. Preliminary reports indicate material damage, with no injuries reported," Bahrain said in a statement. Nov 21, 12:45 PM 2 tankers hit by projectiles whilst exiting the Strait, UKMTO says The UK's Maritime Trade Operations said two tankers were struck separately by unknown projectiles early Saturday while exiting the Strait of Hormuz. One tanker was hit in the stern, the other in the engine room, and there were no reported casualties, the UKMTO said. Separately, Iran's semi-official state media Tasnim News Agency report that a tanker hit a naval mine east of the Strait of Hormuz before noon Saturday and caught fire. Razieh Poudat/ISNA via WANA via Reuters - PHOTO: Vessels are shown in the Strait of Hormuz near the beach of Bandar Abbas, Iran, Nov. 16, 2026. Tasnim, citing the Iranian navy, said the tanker "had entered the restricted area east of the Strait of Hormuz by turning off the identification and navigation systems." "We warn the owners and operators of oil tankers that traffic in the prohibited areas and declared limits is a serious threat to the lives of the crew and the safety of the vessels," the Iranian navy said. Nov 21, 12:25 PM US denies IRGC claim it struck and damaged an F-16 jet over the Gulf U.S. Central Command denied claims by Iran's IRGC that it targeted and damaged a U.S. F-16 fighter aircraft on Friday, forcing an emergency landing. In a post on X, CENTCOM said the claim is false and that "all U.S. military fighter jets in the Middle East are safe and accounted for." US Navy - PHOTO: U.S. sailors conduct flight operations aboard Nimitz-class aircraft carrier USS George H.W. Bush, Nov. 10, 2026. Nov 20, 2:31 PM Saudis, Houthis continue to exchange threats Saudi Arabia and the Iranian-backed Houthis in Yemen continued to exchange escalating threats and strikes on Friday, according to both sides. The Iranian-backed Houthis in Yemen threatened a Saudi power station and Red Sea ports, including Jeddah, according to statements from the Houthis. Recently, the Houthis struck inside of Riyadh’s financial center, causing damage to the Public Investment Fund tower, the headquarters of Saudi Arabia’s sovereign wealth fund and Riyadh’s tallest skyscraper, Saudi Arabia's Civil Defense confirmed. "We declare that the financial center in King Abdullah Economic City in Riyadh, the capital of the enemy Saudi Arabia, is a military target for our forces. Therefore, we call on all employees, workers, and citizens to stay away from it immediately," the Houthis warned in a statement. This incident comes after the Saudi-led coalition said it hit the Houthi-held Hodeidah port and Sanaa. The Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted and destroyed Houthi missiles and military targets in alerts Friday. In a security alert, Maritime security firm Marisks warned that the announcements represent a "significant escalation in Houthi threats." "The announcements represent a significant escalation in Houthi threats against Saudi maritime and energy infrastructure, reinforcing the maritime restrictions previously declared against Saudi-affiliated shipping on July 20th. The possibility of attacks against Saudi ports, energy installations and Saudi-owned, managed or affiliated vessels operating in the Red Sea remains elevated," Marisks wrote. -ABC News' Desiree Adib Nov 20, 2:05 PM 'Watch my lips,' Trump invokes Bush in talking about Iran war President Donald Trump vowed to never let Iran have a nuclear weapon, referencing George H. W. Bush, while giving a press conference at the White House Friday. "We're not going to let them have a nuclear weapon. Iran, I say it, I'll say it now -- and I'm not George Bush -- Watch my lips. No, you don't have to watch my lips. But Iran will never have a nuclear weapon, ever," Trump said. Kylie Cooper/Reuters - PHOTO: President Donald Trump speaks during a news briefing in the James S. Brady Press Briefing Room of the White House, November 20, 2026 in Washington. While accepting the nomination at the 1988 Republican National Convention, Bush famously said the phrase: "Read my lips: no new taxes." Click here to read the rest of the blog. item.title: Trump orders federal contractors to notify White House of congressional inquiries
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
President Donald Trump signed an executive order requiring federal contractors to inform the administration of congressional inquiries into their work with the executive branch as the White House seeks to limit oversight by Democrats. The order, signed Friday, comes after White House Counsel Will Scharf previously instructed all executive agencies to obtain explicit permission from the White House before allowing employees to testify before Congress, according to a memo obtained by ABC News on Monday. Eloisa Lopez/Reuters - PHOTO: President Donald Trump attends an arrival ceremony at Malacanang Palace in Manila, Philippines, November 18, 2026. Federal contractors and subcontractors will now be required to immediately notify the White House and their contracting agencies of "any pending or future congressional request respecting the contractors' communications or work with the executive branch," the order states. All contractors must follow orders from the administration with regard to withholding communications it deems protected by executive privilege. Top White House lawyer warns Democrats that threats of oversight could be criminally probed According to the order, contractors who fail to notify the White House of requests from Congress or refuse to follow the administration's instructions face potential contract termination, as well as suspension or debarment, which would prevent a contractor from winning future federal contracts. "The ability of the Congress to seek executive branch information is limited; it cannot seek information from executive branch departments and agencies (agencies), employees, or Federal contractors without a valid legislative purpose that does not intrude on core Executive functions," the order signed by Trump states. The executive order does not name a specific contractor, but covers "all federal contractors," and extends that coverage to "subcontractors working for a federal contractor on a federal contract." Alex Brandon/AP Photo - PHOTO: President Donald Trump talks after visiting the White House Ballroom construction site at the White House, Nov. 4, 2026, in Washington, D.C. There are roughly 100,000 companies that hold federal contracts, plus the subcontractors, according to Bloomberg Government . The order argues that a "lack of coordination" between the administration and its contractors undermines efficiency and claims that "contractors also may be unaware of the executive branch's interests and positions, resulting in duplicative and wasteful efforts." "It is therefore the policy of the United States to protect confidential information and enhance economy and efficiency in Federal contracting by preventing and prohibiting uncoordinated disclosures of information pursuant to congressional requests," the order states. The White House's Office of Management and Budget will develop guidelines to ensure compliance and "adequate coordination between the contracting agencies, contractors, and White House," the order said. Alex Brandon/AP Photo - PHOTO: President Donald Trump speaks during a tour of the White House Ballroom at the White House, Nov. 4, 2026, in Washington, D.C. In a fact sheet released on Friday by the White House, the administration argued that it "must be able to work closely with its employees and contractors on sensitive matters without concern that confidential information may be released to unauthorized third parties, even by federal contractors from a congressional request." "If the Executive Branch cannot be assured that communications with contractors will remain confidential, federal agencies will be deterred from safely and freely sharing sensitive information with them, which will deadlock critical government programs," it added. Democrats take the House. Here’s what they plan to investigate and their legislative agenda The order marks yet another attempt to push back on potential oversight of the White House, as Congressional Democrats have warned that they are preparing to launch new investigations. Incoming House Oversight Committee Chair Robert Garcia warned the administration to "lawyer up" in the wake of November's elections. Finn Gomez/Getty Images - PHOTO: President Donald Trump speaks during a news briefing in the James S. Brady Press Briefing Room of the White House, November 20, 2026 in Washington. In a letter sent to the California Democratic lawmaker last week, Scharf warned that Democrats could be criminally probed over their threats of exercising Congress's oversight powers, claiming that "abusive threats and public statements about the indiscriminate issuance of subpoenas ... make it abundantly clear that any forthcoming investigative processes will be deployed to harass and aggrandize, rather than to advance any legitimate legislative end." Garcia responded to the letter last week, saying in a statement that "Congress has wide latitude to conduct investigations and oversight, an authority inherent in the power to legislate." "We are a co-equal branch of government and will not be deterred by baseless threats from a weaponized DOJ or from the President’s lawyers," he added. This article originally appeared on ABC News at https://abcnews.com/Politics/trump-orders-federal-contractors-coordinate-white-house-congressional/story?id=138344717

item.title: Schumer's big Senate victory hasn't silenced Democrats who want him replaced
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By Nolan D. McCaskill WASHINGTON, Nov 22 (Reuters) - Chuck Schumer led Senate Democrats through November's midterm elections that gave them a decisive 56-seat majority. Progressives responded with a collective "thank you, next," arguing he should now make way for a successor. Critics say Schumer's decades in Washington, his age and his close ties to the ‌party establishment make him ill-suited to lead a caucus increasingly shaped by younger, anti-establishment lawmakers. "We write first to thank you," leaders of the populist Working Families Party, ‌which backs like-minded Democratic candidates in elections, said in a November 13 letter to Schumer that called for a generational leadership change. "If you step aside at the height of a victory you helped secure, you would show voters ​that the Democratic Party heeded their call for change. The new majority can begin its work united and focused on fighting for the people who elected them." The top Democrat in the Senate for the past decade, Schumer, who turns 76 on Monday, has projected confidence that his colleagues will choose to keep him as their leader in a secret vote on December 1. "I will be elected majority leader," Schumer, who is strongly favored to win, told reporters matter-of-factly last week. But in the first contested Senate Democratic leadership race since 1994, the New York senator faces a challenge from ‌Senator Chris Van Hollen, 67. While only modestly younger than Schumer, ⁠the Maryland lawmaker and his progressive allies outside the Capitol have cast him as an agent of change. Van Hollen has said the 2026 results show voters are demanding the party break with the status quo and adopt a bolder approach that gives new voices, including incoming progressive lawmakers, more ⁠influence in the caucus. 'TIME FOR NEW IDEAS' The Maryland Democrat has run an increasingly public campaign, though the outcome will be determined in private by 56 Senate Democrats. At least 16 Democrats have publicly committed to backing Schumer, while only six have said they will vote for Van Hollen. "I'm in this to win it," Van Hollen said on Thursday. "That's my goal. I think if we want to move forward on an ambitious ​agenda ​like this, we need new leadership. We need to change the culture of the Democratic caucus. People need ​to have more input. Our new members need to be at ‌the table." Democrats flipped nine Senate seats in November, including in several states President Donald Trump won by double digits in 2024. Many of the incoming freshmen said during their campaigns that they would oppose Schumer for Democratic leader. "Do I like Chuck Schumer?" asked Senator-elect Troy Jackson of Maine. "He's been great, but I do think it's time for new ideas." In an interview last week on CNN's "State of the Union," Van Hollen cited a "hunger for change" among Senate Democrats and said two incoming senators won despite Schumer's efforts to back their primary opponents. He criticized Schumer for aligning with powerful pro-Israel and cryptocurrency interests in those races. PROGRESSIVES BACK VAN HOLLEN Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan said Van Hollen stands out because he understands how Washington and the Senate work as a past ‌chair of House and Senate Democrats' respective campaign arms, and he's willing to take risks. "Those two things ​are what we need right now, and we need to rethink the way we legislate," he said, pointing to ​Van Hollen's trips to advocate for a wrongly deported migrant and to draw ​attention to Israel's war in Gaza as examples of his willingness to take risks. Senator Tim Kaine of Virginia suggested the leadership fight reflected a healthy ‌discussion within the caucus about its future direction. "And there's nothing wrong with ​that," he told Reuters. Senate Democratic leader is the ​only unresolved role among Congress' top four positions. House Democrats last week nominated Hakeem Jeffries to be speaker in the next Congress, where John Thune will continue to lead Senate Republicans and Representative Jim Jordan will succeed Speaker Mike Johnson as the top House Republican. SCHUMER COULD FACE PRIMARY CHALLENGER IN 2028 Schumer is up for reelection in 2028, ​and losing the leadership race could make him a more vulnerable ‌target, as ambitious Democrats such as Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez consider running for his seat. A memo from Ocasio-Cortez's campaign acknowledged she could run for president, Senate or reelection to ​the House in 2028. For his part, Schumer has swatted down questions about his future beyond the leadership election. "I'm focused on 2027 and delivering for the American ​people," he said on Wednesday. (Reporting by Nolan D. McCaskill; Editing by Michael Learmonth and Cynthia Osterman) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://www.yahoo.com/news/articles/schumer-led-democrats-big-senate-110533108.html

item.title: Water supply hack warning: FBI says threats are rising
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
( NewsNation ) — Recent cyber outages have disrupted airlines, retailers and hospitals, but experts warn the next major target could be something far more essential: the water coming from your tap. Federal agencies, researchers and cybersecurity experts are sounding alarms about rising threats to U.S. water systems as hackers increasingly target vulnerable infrastructure connected to the Internet. Why are officials worried now? The FBI warned in July that malicious cyber actors have been targeting Internet-facing programmable logic controllers, or PLCs, used by water and wastewater systems. According to the FBI, these intrusions have already caused operational disruptions, highlighting how vulnerable critical infrastructure can be when equipment is exposed online. Government advisor says Doomsday supply stockers aren’t overreacting How serious is the threat? The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency warned in September that cyberattacks against public water systems are increasing. The agency says utilities face threats ranging from ransomware to sophisticated intrusions that could disrupt operations or affect service reliability. What are local governments facing? A recent report from The Pew Charitable Trusts found that many drinking water and wastewater systems operate with aging technology, limited budgets and staffing shortages that can hinder cybersecurity efforts. Pew reported that local governments are increasingly investing in cyber defenses, but many smaller systems still struggle to keep pace with evolving threats. How is AI changing the risk landscape? Researchers Susan Athey, Neil Gandal, and Tyler Moore at Stanford Graduate School of Business say in their report "A Wake-Up Call on Cyber Risk as AI Ups the Stakes" that artificial intelligence is accelerating the cyber threat environment by helping attackers identify vulnerabilities more quickly and execute attacks at greater scale. "The most severe cyber incidents can lead to losses amounting to billions of dollars and also have the potential to result in physical harm, loss of life, or even political turmoil," they state in the report. Rubio on tech failures: US ‘not under systemic attack’ Why are experts calling this a wake-up call? According to a recent Time analysis , cyberattacks have already affected water facilities in several states, including an incident in Minnesota that disrupted equipment at a treatment plant and threatened the local water supply. Many small water systems remain vulnerable because they lack dedicated cybersecurity resources, making resilience and emergency preparedness increasingly important as threats grow. Bolton sounds alarm after Microsoft, FAA outages What can utilities do? Federal guidance urges utilities to strengthen cyber hygiene by disconnecting unnecessary Internet-facing devices, implementing multifactor authentication, conducting regular vulnerability assessments and maintaining incident response plans. The FBI and EPA have encouraged operators to monitor industrial control systems closely and promptly apply security updates when available. What can people do at home? Experts say households should prepare for potential service disruptions much like they would for severe weather or power outages. That can include maintaining an emergency supply of bottled water, storing water safely for sanitation needs, keeping basic emergency kits and monitoring instructions from local authorities if a utility reports an incident. NewsNation's Jesse Weber recently spoke with preparedness expert Jim Cobb, who said, "My longstanding recommendation has always been have enough cash immediately accessible" for fuel, lodging and meals during an emergency. Cobb also advised households to review supplies already on hand before rushing to stores, adding that food, water and basic necessities should be a priority. Microsoft outage raises concerns over US cybersecurity Why does this matter beyond cybersecurity? Water systems are among the most critical pieces of infrastructure in the country, serving millions of Americans every day. While major cyberattacks remain relatively rare, federal officials, researchers and industry experts agree that growing digital threats, combined with increasingly connected systems, mean cybersecurity is no longer just an IT problem. It is becoming a public safety issue. Copyright 2026 Nexstar Media, Inc. All rights reserved. This material may not be published, broadcast, rewritten, or redistributed. For the latest news, weather, sports, and streaming video, head to NewsNation. This article originally appeared on NewsNation at https://www.newsnationnow.com/cybersecurity/water-supply-warning-fbi-threats-rising/

item.title: Army plans Tuesday detonation of 5 tons of explosives in Iowa as court fight continues
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
A sign sits on top of a building at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant on Thursday in Middletown, Iowa. - Scott Olson/Getty Images The US Army intends to detonate nearly five tons of lead azide at an Iowa munitions plant by Tuesday, even though a federal appeals court has paused its permit, by invoking an emergency exemption it says allows it to act without one, the Justice Department told the court in a filing Saturday . The court’s order “does not enjoin or otherwise prohibit the Army from acting under a separate legal authority,” the Justice Department argued. The Army says the degraded material could explode on its own as temperatures drop. “The real choice, in other words, is not between a detonation and no detonation. It is between a planned and mitigated detonation and an unplanned and unmitigated explosion,” the filing said. A federal appeals court temporarily paused the US Environmental Protection Agency permit that would allow the Army to detonate the material at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in tiny Middletown on Thursday after environmental groups sued. The detonation, originally scheduled for Friday morning, had been moved to Monday. The Justice Department has “laid the groundwork for a possible detonation without a permit, which would effectively bypass judicial process and review,” Rachel Rintelmann, a managing attorney at Earthjustice, which represents the environmental groups, said in an email Saturday. The Army, in coordination with the EPA, plans to destroy nearly 70 drums of lead azide, a compound used to detonate munitions, the military branch said. The plan has drawn heavy pushback from concerned Iowans, environmental advocates and politicians who worry the plume could spread toxic lead dust – unhealthy at any level and especially dangerous to children – over vast swaths of rural Iowa, the Mississippi River and potentially part of western Illinois. Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds on Friday activated a state emergency operations center, while officials in nearby Illinois are warning residents about dust spilling over into their state. The Federal Aviation Administration has restricted flights around Middletown from Monday through Wednesday, according to a temporary flight restriction notice . Here’s what we know about the planned detonation and the legal fight. Army says detonation is needed The Army in March , during “ routine stockpile surveillance,” discovered lead azide housed in bunkers had been degrading, according to Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle. Officials evaluating the best way to dispose of the material communicated with “stakeholders and the public in Middletown and the modeled impact area about the danger it posed,” Telle said. The lead azide’s degraded status left it “extremely unstable and sensitive to even slight friction or movement,” according to an FAQ distributed by the Army to the community last month. “Packing and transporting it poses an unacceptable risk of accidental detonation to personnel handling and transporting as well as to the public.” After coordinating with the EPA, experts and the community, officials “determined that a controlled detonation was the option that posed the lowest risk to the public in the immediate and surrounding area,” Telle said. Army officials held an October 15 community meeting to share information about a potential detonation in late November, according to documents on the plant’s page . Then, on November 15, the community got a notice of a detonation on Friday, according to an Army news release . After pushback, the Army rescheduled the detonation to Monday – the “latest possible moment prior to a forecasted temperature drop, which would risk further destabilization of the material,” Telle said. While noting the court’s pause is still in place, the City of Fort Madison said Saturday it was notified that the detonation would most likely occur either Monday or Tuesday, but if it doesn’t happen this week, “another time will need to be arranged with additional planning.” CNN has reached out to the city for additional information. Waiting too long to detonate the lead azide could pose more hazards later, he said. The emergency permit from the EPA would allow the Army to do the detonation between November 13 and February 11, 2027. Still, the problem should have been evaluated 20 years ago, said Patrick O’Shaughnessy, a University of Iowa professor and environmental health expert. “Somebody left it to rot that long, for it to now being the only option is to blow it up on site because it can’t be moved,” he told CNN. “It’s regrettable, and it’s almost, it’s hard to believe that it’s happening in this country.” The Army had previously awarded a contract to MuniRem Environmental, a Georgia-based firm that uses chemicals to neutralize munitions, but later canceled the deal citing safety concerns, the New York Times reported, and instead opted to detonate the lead azide. The Times said the Army did not respond to questions about the canceled deal. The outlet cited Valentine Nzengung, a chief executive at MuniRem, who said the Army did not give a reason for the cancellation, and that then-Army Secretary Dan Driscoll had made the final determination that the controlled detonation would take place instead. The Times said it reviewed emails that show an Army contracting officer telling the company that the decision “was not based on deficiencies” in MuniRem’s proposed technical approach. CNN has reached out to the Army for comment. Nzengung told CNN the Army “told us that they evaluated reports and they found out that controlled detonation was the safest way, and that is why they were moving forward with controlled detonation. They did not provide us much more detail than this.” Iowans, local officials and environmental groups push back Officials at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant have regularly updated officials in Middletown – home to 363 people – about the planned detonation, according to Brieanna Beck, the city clerk and municipal officer, who said she has quickly shared each update on the city’s Facebook page. The city has been aware of the detonation plan for a couple of months, she told CNN in an email. The Army plant sent letters to homes potentially affected by the detonation, Beck said. The governor’s office and state agencies were coordinating with EPA and Army officials to “continuously monitor the situation and keep local partners informed,” Reynolds said Friday. More than 80 miles north of Middletown, Cedar Rapids is preparing for the detonation. Officials in Iowa’s second-most populous city are taking steps to monitor the drinking water supply – drawn from wells along the Cedar River – for potential contamination, though they don’t anticipate impacts, according to a city update . But plans and communication around the detonation have gotten strong pushback from environmental advocates, as well as state and federal politicians in Iowa and neighboring Illinois. Josh Turek, the US senator-elect for Iowa, has called for a delay to the detonation, saying he had “heard from many Iowans who are worried about their health and safety due to the potential risk of lead exposure as a result of the detonation.” Rob Sand, the incoming governor, said Iowans’ safety now and in the future should be the government’s top concern. “An unacceptable lack of communication and clarity has made Iowans understandably concerned and angry about this situation,” he said . “The public deserves to know, if this is the safest option, why other options were worse.” Parts of western and central Illinois could be affected by the lead plume under the current weather forecast, Illinois state officials said in an update Friday. Illinois health and environmental protection officials said they are monitoring the planned detonation and have issued updates to residents. Illinois agriculture officials have issued guidance to protect livestock and pets. They recommended keeping animals inside until the plume has passed and washing them to remove potential contaminants. Meanwhile, officials warned of exposure through fishing. Residents should stay indoors on the detonation day, with windows and doors closed for one to two days after as a precaution, Illinois officials said. They also encouraged people to use portable air cleaners equipped with a HEPA filter. Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker said Friday he had spoken with Telle, urging more transparency about the planned detonation. “The State is still seeking more data from them on how this could impact Illinoisans and is working to keep you informed and safe,” Pritzker said . What the court has said Environmental advocates sued the US EPA on Thursday over the emergency permit allowing the Army to detonate the lead azide, citing concerns about the potential impacts of the explosion. The Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals on Thursday temporarily stayed the EPA’s emergency permit until it rules on the groups’ emergency motion, but didn’t say when the court would take action on the case. The EPA signaled in an earlier court filing it planned to file a response by Sunday. The Army, in a joint statement with the US Department of Health and Human Services and the EPA, said Friday afternoon, “The entire interagency is working together to ensure that the controlled detonation in Middletown, Iowa, is conducted in the safest fashion possible.” “Officials have been meticulously planning for this event since March, and all agencies involved are prepared to take the most extreme mitigation measures available to ensure there is no risk to the public and any disruptions are minimized,” the statement said, adding they will keep local officials and the public updated. The cleanup requirements under the current permit are inadequate to properly address the scope and degree of potential impacts, according to Thien Chau, a senior attorney at the environmental advocacy nonprofit Earthjustice, who filed the lawsuit on behalf of the Iowa Environmental Council and the Sierra Club Iowa Chapter. There doesn’t appear to be sufficient understanding of how far the plume would spread, as well as which bodies of water, such as the Mississippi River, and land would be blanketed with lead dust, including where people live, Chau told reporters Friday. Environmental advocates called on state leaders, including Reynolds, to take control of communication over the planned detonation. The federal government, including the Army and EPA, couldn’t be trusted to adequately inform Iowans about the risks of the planned detonation, Michael Schmidt, general counsel at the Iowa Environmental Council, said in a news briefing. “Iowans deserve a transparent, coordinated, and effective response to this unprecedented event,” Schmidt said. In Saturday’s filing, the Justice Department cited a federal regulation that exempts responses to an “immediate threat” to human health, public safety, property or the environment from EPA permitting requirements. Col. Aaron Teller, commander of the Army’s 71st Ordnance Group, which handles explosive ordnance disposal, determined the lead azide poses “an immediate threat,” according to a sworn declaration filed with the notice. The Justice Department has not responded to CNN’s request for comment. “We want to be absolutely clear that the regulation they cite is an extraordinary and extreme backstop for situations where there is truly nothing else that can be done,” Rintelmann said. “It is an incredibly high bar, and we urge the Army not to rely on it if it is only doing so to sidestep the ongoing processes to obtain transparency and protections that communities, government leaders, and the law demand.” Health risks of lead exposure There is no safe level of lead in the body, Dr. Sameer Vohra, director of the Illinois Department of Public Health, said in a statement . “(And) when inhaled or swallowed, it can pose serious health risks.” With the detonation, the hope is if the lead azide spreads over a wider area, it won’t stay in high-level concentrations, according to O’Shaughnessy, the University of Iowa professor. “It’s kind of like one of these, the solution to pollution is dilution, right?” he said. There is the potential for exposure through the air during the initial plume or through touch after it has settled, he said, adding neither exposure is worse than the other because the lead will still build up in your body both ways. Lead is toxic to the brain. Exposure is known to cause serious harm to children’s health, resulting in slowed growth and development, as well as problems with learning, behavior, hearing and speech, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention . Environmental advocates also warn the detonation could worsen health for residents in Iowa, which has the second-highest rate of cancer of any US state and is one of only three states where the rate is rising. The local National Weather Service office forecasts cooler, drier conditions early this week, with highs in the upper 30s to the mid-40s. Wind conditions could affect how far lead particles travel, and winds are forecast to blow from north to south at around 5 to 10 mph, CNN meteorologist Chris Dolce said. CNN’s Holly Yan, Kara Devlin and Bill Kirkos contributed to this report. For more CNN news and newsletters create an account at CNN.com This article originally appeared on CNN at https://www.cnn.com/2026/11/21/us/iowa-army-detonation-what-we-know

item.title: 'Saturday Night Live' 'Sister' sketch shows the real cost of 'free' caregiving
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The most popular caregiving service in America has no website, no waitlist and no price tag. "Saturday Night Live" finally gave it a name: Sister. In the parody commercial , comedian John Mulaney plays a man who is desperate to find care for his aging dad but can’t afford a private aide. Then he discovers Sister. She offers around-the-clock care, manages medications, handles doctor's appointments and best of all, costs nothing. Signing up takes a two-word text: "Dad fell." With "Sister," "Saturday Night Live" did what it does best: It made us laugh by taking something we’ve come to accept and showing us how absurd it is. Here, it’s a care system built on the assumption that Sister will "quit her job, break her lease and move halfway across the country" to take care of Dad. Satire usually exaggerates the truth. For millions of women, "Sister" hit home because it barely had to. In case you missed it: What is caregiver creep? The slippery slope of 'just helping out' What played out as a three-minute comedy sketch reflects unequal expectations that shape years of women's lives, with sacrifices they’re expected to make without question. More than half of family caregivers − 56% − felt they had no choice but to take on the responsibility, according to the Caregiving in the US 2025 report from AARP and the National Alliance for Caregiving. Women make up 61% of the country’s 63 million family caregivers, and nearly 1 in 4 provides around-the-clock care. But just because there isn’t an invoice doesn’t mean Sister’s care is free. Their unpaid care is worth more than $643 billion annually , according to an analysis from The National Partnership for Women & Families, including more than $268 billion contributed by Black women, Latinas and Asian women. And that doesn’t begin to capture what they give up along the way: wages, promotions, savings and retirement security. Women caregivers lose an average of $9,400 in lifetime Social Security income, AARP found, compared with $6,800 for men. And across all family caregivers, out-of-pocket spending now averages more than $11,500 a yea r, up nearly 60% since 2021. That is the care system we call free. Care comes with a cost. Eldest daughters know it all too well And the price isn't measured in dollars alone. So many caregivers delay their own doctor's appointments because there simply aren't enough hours in the day. They’re physically and mentally exhausted − coordinating care, navigating insurance, managing emergencies, preparing meals − while neglecting their own needs. In fact, more than one in four women caregivers struggle to take care of their own health. The sketch makes it easy to criticize brothers who rely on their sisters. But the real joke is bigger than any one family. America has built a care system that depends on someone, usually a woman, stepping in to do whatever it takes, regardless of what it costs , without offering any support. For too many families, the care plan is not really a plan at all. It’s whoever can rearrange their life first. No one should have to sacrifice their livelihood, health or future because a loved one needs care. The solution isn’t simply dividing responsibilities more fairly within our families − it’s passing policies that ease the burden and make support more readily available to everyone who needs it. The problem is structural, not individual − and it’s only getting worse. More Americans are living longer, and millions more will need care in the years ahead. But our care system is struggling to keep up. Worker shortages and long wait lists already make help difficult to find. Meanwhile, recent cuts to Medicaid, the largest payer for home care, threaten to further limit those services and leave families responsible for shouldering even more care. There are ways to change this. Congress can save caregivers money and time, and provide more support through common-sense policy. Tax credits like those in Oklahoma, Connecticut and Nebraska could offset the thousands of dollars families spend out of pocket. Paid family and medical leave would give someone time to tend to a loved one without losing a paycheck. And stronger home care services would give families more reliable options when they need help. We need a system that recognizes how essential care is to our lives and gives families the support they deserve. When we invest in caregivers , we invest in our economic strength as a country. We laughed at "Saturday Night Live" because we recognized Sister. She’s our mother, our daughter , our neighbor, our co-worker. Maybe she’s us. But behind the laughter is something we can no longer afford to ignore. What happens when Sister needs care? Who takes her to appointments? Who manages her medications? The wages and savings she sacrifices today may be what she needs to afford her own care tomorrow. Meanwhile, paying for a parent’s care can drain the savings and inheritance that might have helped protect her future. And the cost of doing nothing gets passed from one generation to the next . At a time when affordability is the buzz word looming over every national debate, strengthening support for caregivers ought to be top of mind. The people who care for everyone else deserve a future where they’re cared for, too. We cannot simply hope there’s another Sister waiting to answer the text. Dr. Myechia Minter-Jordan is CEO of AARP. Ai-jen Poo is co-founder and executive director of Caring Across Generations. item.title: Families of troops killed in Kuwait strike say Pentagon probe leaves questions unanswered
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Gold Star families have told CBS News that briefings about a forthcoming U.S. military report on the deadliest strike on U.S. soldiers in the Iran conflict did not, to their satisfaction, address their concerns about the military preparations and response to the attack. Several of the families said they have been briefed about the unclassified results from the long-awaited internal probe into one of the first attacks on U.S. troops during Operation Epic Fury. Six U.S. Army Reserve soldiers were killed by a drone strike on their command post in Kuwait, known as Port Shuaiba, on March 1. The official report has not yet been released to the public. The Pentagon has indicated it could be made public in a matter of days. Over the past week, the Army briefed at least three Gold Star families on the investigation, and several family members told CBS News they were frustrated by what they heard. Some of those briefed told CBS News the report does little to address the findings of an eight-month CBS News investigation, in which multiple sources said Army commanders ignored repeated warnings about the drone threat in the weeks before the attack. Witnesses told CBS News that the facilities were not fortified to protect service members from a strike by one-way attack drones, which are a staple of the Iranian arsenal. Soldiers on the site said they had seen U.S. intelligence prior to the war showing the location was on an Iranian target list. And they argued the facilities lacked sufficient medical supplies and a plan for a mass casualty incident. The briefings were led by Brig. Gen. Peter Glass, the deputy commander of U.S. Army Central, according to those who attended. They were individually held at either military or National Guard posts in locations close to the respective families. "I wish I felt better," a Gold Star family member told CBS News after her briefing, which she said lasted roughly three hours. "I wish this gave me more than what I had yesterday or what I had the day before." The briefings come just days after a U.S. Army soldier who survived the deadly Iranian drone attack filed a whistleblower complaint to Congress alleging senior military officials ignored warnings and did not plan properly for anti-drone defenses ahead of the war with Iran. The whistleblower, Army Maj. Stephen Ramsbottom, spoke exclusively with 60 Minutes' Norah O'Donnell about his complaint, which was submitted to the House and Senate Armed Services Committees on Nov. 13 and obtained by CBS News. In the complaint, Ramsbottom alleges that Army leaders were warned about drone threats at the U.S. command post, and alleges the site had "no dedicated protection" against the Iranian drones. In an interview with CBS News, he identified Brig. Gen. Clint Barnes, who commanded the unit, and Maj. Gen. John Hinson, who oversaw logistics for the U.S. command, as dismissing warnings about protection at the location. Ramsbottom called for an independent investigation. Neither official responded to multiple requests for comment from CBS News. Another Gold Star family member described the briefing as mostly "cordial" but said the exchange grew tense when family members pressed for more answers about why the unit was moved to Port Shuaiba when most other soldiers were sent out of Kuwait ahead of the launch of Operation Epic Fury. "We took a couple breaks because it got heavy and I needed some air," one family member said. Joey Amor, whose wife, Master Sgt. Nicole Amor, was among those killed, told 60 Minutes he believes she might have survived if there was a better plan in place. "I think my wife had a shot, yeah," he said. He said investigators told him that, no matter what medical resources were present, his wife's injuries were too severe for her to have survived the strike. The Pentagon for months has declined comment to CBS News, but confirmed its internal investigation into the Port Shuaiba attack concluded in June. Still, it would take until mid-November for the Army to share its findings — another point of contention for some Gold Star family members. "Going in I had an idea of what I wanted to know," another family member said. "I just knew I wasn't going to get answers — and I was right." The FBI did not immediately respond to a request for comment about the cyberattack, which was first reported by CNN on Friday . item.title: Abdul El-Sayed catches Trump's attention with pitch for 'Trumpcare'
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed pitched for universal healthcare to be called “Trumpcare" in an effort to grab the president's attention. (Sarah Rice / Getty) President Donald Trump responded on Saturday to Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed’s push for universal healthcare after the progressive Michigan Democrat pitched that it be called “Trumpcare.” “Donald, this is on the table,” El-Sayed wrote in a post on X last week. “Guarantee healthcare for every American, from cradle to grave.” El-Sayed, a former public health official who made Medicare for All a cornerstone of his campaign, included mock images of “Trumpcare” cards in the post. The cards are branded with the title named after the president and are golden, an homage to Trump’s favorite color. Trump reposted a screenshot of El-Sayed’s post on Truth Social Saturday, though he didn’t include any text with it. However, he said in a phone interview with Fox News earlier in the day that he believes the government could “do tremendous things on healthcare” after Democrats take control of Congress in January. “They have some good points on healthcare, and they have some bad points, and we have some good things, and probably they would say we have some bad things,” Trump said, referring to congressional Democrats. “But there’s a chance we could get great healthcare and a lot of other things, and we do it in a bipartisan way.” Trump also told reporters at a press conference Friday that he is “open to great healthcare.” “There’s a real possibility that we get a lot of great things done, especially on healthcare,” he said. “It can be a combination of what we all want, and we could end up with great healthcare in our country. We could end up better than dealing with the Republicans.” Despite touting his openness to work with Democrats, Trump has also repeatedly emphasized his power to veto legislation since Republican losses in the midterms. “I’ll get along, probably, with the Democrats unless they want to be destructive,” Trump said the day after the election. “But I have the power of the veto.” Trump did say in the interview with Fox News on Saturday that he does not think that vetoing “everything” passed by Democrats for the next two years is the way to go. But he also posted another image of himself on Truth Social later in the day, showing him in a red “VETO”-branded hat and a matching jacket. In a statement Saturday afternoon, El-Sayed said he is “happy to chat” with the president if his intentions to work together on healthcare are genuine. “If the President is serious about meeting the unmet promise of guaranteed healthcare in this country, I’m ready to work alongside leaders in the Senate like Senators Van Hollen, Sanders, Wyden, and Warren to deliver,” El-Sayed said. “President Trump, give me a call.” This article was originally published on NBCNews.com This article originally appeared on NBC News at https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/donald-trump/abdul-el-sayed-catches-trumps-attention-pitch-trumpcare-rcna610626

item.title: World's longest climate summit ends without a deal after fossil fuel dispute
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The Cop31 climate summit in Turkey descended into disarray and disappointment after countries were unable to reach consensus on a deal that failed to mention fossil fuels. Nations rejected the agreement at a fraught closing session in Antalya on Sunday, almost two days after the summit was due to finish in what stretched to become the longest Cop in history. The European Union , the UK and small island states such as Tuvalu refused to accept the text over the absence of fossil fuels, blasting the omissions as “greenwashing” and accusing oil states of “hijacking” the talks. Ireland’s minister for climate Darragh O’Brien, speaking on behalf of the EU, called the text “unconscionable” and said its ambition went “nowhere near the level of action that's required to deal with climate change”. A spokesperson for the British delegation said it was “profoundly disappointed” by the proposed deal. Some nations indicated a willingness to continue working, but at the closing plenary summit president ⁠Murat ​Kurum said ⁠there would be no new ⁠draft of the ​deal. COP31 president Murat Kurum leaves after the final plenary session on the second overtime day on Sunday (Getty) Andy Burnham was the only G7 leader to attend the summit, where he made an impassioned speech promising to usher in a “new era of British leadership" on climate change. But the prime minister said nothing on Sunday as hopes of a deal evaporated and delegates eventually left empty handed. UK energy secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh later called the failure to reach a deal “immensely disappointing” but said there had been “genuine progress” during the conference. “This Cop sought to confront hard truths – that global warming is set to overshoot 1.5C and that we must act with ever more urgency to address it,” she said in a statement. “The moment required bold ambition and we have been working tirelessly to try to build consensus. It is immensely disappointing we have been unable to do so.” The failed deal had acknowledged the planet's projected temperature overshoot for the first time and called for faster development of carbon-removal technologies to eventually reverse it. It was already heavily criticised by small islands and civil society groups who called it a “betrayal” and criticised its reliance on carbon capture schemes, which had been pushed by oil states including Saudi Arabia. "It seems like we are negotiating with the Saudis," Maina Talia, Tuvalu's climate minister, commented during the conference. A representative for the Saudi delegation, which supported the deal's mention of carbon removal, told the summit he was surprised at the ‌resistance to technology, which he said offered a “concrete solution”. Ireland's minister for climate, environment, energy and transport Darragh O'Brien (L) had criticised the draft deal (AFP/Getty) Developing countries had also criticised the deal for not providing sufficient new funds to ​help them adapt to a warming planet. China and India said they had objections but chose to accept the cover text to move things forward. Earlier, Mr Kurum, defended the text and said the presidencies had “listened to everyone” and tried to bring the groups together, but admitted there was “no consensus”. Australia's Cop31 president of negotiations, Chris Bowen, called the outcome "very disappointing" and said disagreements over fuels ​and ⁠climate finance were the dealbreakers. The conference became the longest COP ever on Sunday afternoon, passing COP25 in Madrid in 2019, which ran 44 hours over its schedule. Delegates pored over several drafts with language that tried to bridge the position of countries most exposed to climate impacts and those whose economies depend on producing or consuming fossil fuels, but the split came down to whether the text should refer to oil, gas and coal at all. The first time the transition away from fossil fuels found a mention in a UN climate agreement was at Cop28 in Dubai in 2023. It had been hoped that a series of climate disasters in the lead up to this year’s conference would help to sharpen minds and reaffirm commitments. The last time UN climate talks failed to get a deal adopted by all was in Copenhagen in 2009. Chief executive of environmental charity Friends of the Earth Asad Rehman said the deal in its current form “is no deal at all” and urged governments to pledge more than “wooly” promises. He warned leaders the “clock is ticking” and said governments must “come back to the negotiating table ready to deliver”. United Nationals general secretary Antonio Guterres also said he was "deeply disappointed” by the conference’s failure to reach a consensus. “I share the very profound frustration of all those who expected governments to rise to the moment the climate crisis demands,” he said. "There may be no consensus in the negotiating room. There is no ambiguity in the science." Some campaigners also turned on the EU, which rejected the text while some lauded the resistance shown at the plenary. "The EU is trying to shift blame onto others and it is deeply hypocritical. At the beginning of COP31, it signalled it was prepared to drop the renewables ask from the electrification target and it has failed to put forward an EU fossil fuel transition roadmap," said Laurie van der Burg of Oil Change International. The failure is a blow to efforts to ratchet up international ‌action, but does not erase the obligations agreed by previous ‌summits or remove existing agreements on action against climate change. item.title: For many young people, the path to homeownership means moving in with parents
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
As home prices and mortgage rates remain elevated, young people are trying a new tactic to accelerate their home savings: moving back in with mom and dad. More than 1 in 5 of this year's first-time buyers reported living with parents, relatives, or friends immediately before buying a home, according to National Association of Realtors data, a level that jumped during the pandemic and has remained elevated in the years since. In the 1990s, as few as 12% of buyers had such an arrangement. The uptick comes as a major hurdle to first-time homeownership — saving for a down payment — is getting harder. Higher home prices mean more money down, while rising rents eat into savings rates, slowing down the process. One study by the Center for Responsible Lending's Julian Bond Institute found that the time it takes a typical renter family to save for a down payment doubled from 8 to 16 years between 2019 and 2026. The appeal of living at home is obvious: Housing costs are the single largest line item on most budgets, and parents are often happy to let their children live rent-free or at below-market rates. "It's a great way to save up money," said Jeff Silver, a mortgage loan officer with Big Valley Mortgage in Roseville, Calif. Read more: How housing trends differ across Gen Z, millennials, Gen X, and boomers He counsels clients in rent-free living situations to make "pretend" mortgage payments straight into their savings accounts. In his area, where the median home lists for nearly $650,000, he rarely sees monthly home payments below $3,800. Saving that for a year would bring in over $45,000 and cover a down payment. More young adults are living at home regardless of whether they're explicitly saving for a home. As of last year, roughly 1 in 3 adults under 35 lived with their parents, just off of all-time highs reached during the early days of the pandemic. "I somewhat view it positively," Lawrence Yun, the NAR's chief economist, said of young people who are living at home and stockpiling cash instead of renting. "A down payment is one of the major barriers to getting into that first level." Young adults who choose to move back home to fast-track their savings are trading away some short-term independence in hopes of a healthy long-term financial future. And for parents or relatives looking for ways to help children get a foothold into an expensive market, offering up a spare bedroom can be a powerful alternative to a direct cash gift. Ruthie Bult, 26, and her husband moved in with her parents in New Hampshire shortly after she gave birth to their now 1-year-old son. They had hoped to stay just a few months while hunting for a home nearby, but found little available inventory and a competitive market. They've now lived with her parents for almost a year. "They know the state of the housing market," she said of her parents. "They're not pressuring us or rushing us into something that wouldn't be the right situation." It's not the living situation Bult envisioned for this stage of her life, but it's one she's made peace with for the sake of her family's future finances. "We would have so much less saved for a house and for our retirement and all of that if we were in an apartment or renting a house," she said. And there have been other perks too, like the extra help she gets caring for her son, and the close bond he's developed with his grandparents. Now armed with a year's worth of savings, she and her husband plan to restart their house hunt in the coming months. They aim to find a multifamily unit that they can live in while also having renters to further defray their mortgage expenses. "We're sacrificing now with the hopes that in the long run, we'll be able to go straight into our own place and invest more in ourselves," she said. Claire Boston is a senior reporter for Yahoo Finance covering housing, mortgages, and home insurance. item.title: Trump says he would work with Democrats to cap credit card interest rates
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
President Trump said he would work with the incoming Democratic Congress to cap credit card interest rates, hoping to fulfill a promise he made on the 2024 campaign trail but couldn't deliver on because of industry pressure and a lack of interest from his fellow Republicans. "I would do it. These credit card companies have made a lot," Trump told Fox News Channel's "Saturday in America." Democrats and the Republican president have both backed capping credit card interest rates, with the standard proposal being capping rates at 10%. It would substantially reduce what credit card companies can charge customers. The median credit card interest rate is roughly 22.2%, according to an August survey by the New York Federal Reserve. With rates at 10%, a cardholder with a $5,000 balance would pay about $42 per month in interest. At the current average rate of 22%, they would owe about $100 per month. Mr. Trump proposed capping credit card interest rates in January , as part of the White House's affordability push. Banks and credit card companies immediately and aggressively opposed the proposal, saying any interest rate cap would force them to cancel cards for the poor and less creditworthy customers or substantially cut back on the rewards they offer when customers spend on their cards. The proposal also did not sit well with Republicans, and there was little effort by the GOP-controlled Congress to fulfill Mr. Trump's promise. That could change now that Democrats will control both the House and Senate. Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., who is expected to be the next chair of the Senate Banking Committee, has said repeatedly she wants to cap rates . In response to the Fox News interview, Warren said: "Let's cap credit card interest rates and save Americans money." Warren told CBS News in January 2026 that she believes Congress could work with Mr. Trump to cap rates. Researchers who studied Mr. Trump's campaign pledge after it was first announced found that Americans would save roughly $100 billion in interest a year if credit card rates were capped at 10%. The same researchers found that while the credit card industry would take a major hit, it would still be profitable, although credit card rewards and other perks might be scaled back. About 195 million people in the United States had credit cards in 2024 and were assessed $160 billion in interest charges , the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau says. Americans are now carrying more credit card debt than ever, to the tune of about $1.23 trillion, according to figures from the New York Federal Reserve for the third quarter last year.
